1. Use the `Adult Census Income` dataset.  We will predict the income (whether or not it is more than 50k or not) of an adult. Import the dataset.  Partition the data into 80% training and 20% testing.  

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("caret")
set.seed(1234)
df = read_csv("Data/adult_census.csv")  %>% mutate(
    workclass      = factor(workclass),
    education      = factor(education),
    marital.status = factor(marital.status),
    occupation     = factor(occupation),
    relationship   = factor(relationship),
    race           = factor(race),
    sex            = factor(sex),
    native.country = factor(native.country),
    income         = factor(income)
  )
split_index = createDataPartition(df$income, p=.8, list=FALSE)
training = df[split_index, ]
testing = df[-split_index, ]
```


2. Practice Decision Tree.  Do the follows:

```{r}
library(rpart)
```


  - Use `rpart` package, create a decision tree with maximum depth of 3. 
  
```{r}
tree = rpart(income ~ ., data = training, control = rpart.control(maxdepth=3))
```

  
  - Calculate the accuracy of the model on the testing data. Notice that the positive outcome here is not `1` but `>50K` or `<50K`. 
  
  
```{r}
predict = predict(tree, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]
```

  
  - Plot the tree
  
```{r}
library(rattle)
fancyRpartPlot(tree)
```

  
  - Plot the variable importance by the tree
  
```{r}
tree$variable.importance
```

  
3. Create 3 more trees and compare the testing accuracy of these trees, which tree give the highest testing accuracy.

```{r}
tree1 = rpart(income ~ ., data = training, control = rpart.control(maxdepth=1))
tree2 = rpart(income ~ ., data = training, control = rpart.control(maxdepth=2))
tree3 = rpart(income ~ ., data = training, control = rpart.control(maxdepth=3))

predict = predict(tree1, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]

predict = predict(tree2, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]

predict = predict(tree3, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]
```


4. Practice Random Forest.  Do the follows: 

  - Use `randomForest` package, create a random forest of 1000 trees.
  
```{r}
library("randomForest")
forest = randomForest(income ~ ., data = training, ntree=1000)
```

  
  - Calculate the accuracy of the model on the testing data. 
  
```{r}
predict = predict(forest, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]
```

  
  - Plot the variable importance by the forest
  
```{r}
importance(forest)
```


5. Create 3 more forests and compare the testing accuracy of these forests, which forest give the highest testing accuracy.

```{r}
forest1 = randomForest(income ~ ., data = training, ntree=10)
forest2 = randomForest(income ~ ., data = training, ntree=100)
forest3 = randomForest(income ~ ., data = training, ntree=500)

predict = predict(forest1, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]

predict = predict(forest2, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]

predict = predict(forest3, testing, type="class")
confusion = confusionMatrix(data = predict, reference = testing$income, positive = ">50K")
confusion$overal[1]
```


6. What is the best model (in term of testing accuracy) among all models (including trees and forests) you have trained?

```{r}
print("It is actually the forest trained with 100 trees (Accurary .8636 > .863 the next highest.")
print("Its likely that using more tree is potentially slighlty overfitting but forests are robust to overfitting so it has almost 0 actual effect.")
print("It also makes sense the forest are slightly better than the tree as the forest decreases variance and also uses more compute i.e. is just a bunch of simple trees.")
```
